title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 18
paragraphs: It seemed to Artabanus that the dream uttered these threats and was just about to burn out his eyes with hot irons, when with a loud cry he sprang up from the bed. He sat down beside Xerxes and related the whole vision from beginning to end, and then said: “O king, I, as a man who has seen many great things in my time brought to ruin by lesser ones, urged you not to yield in everything to the impulses of your youth, knowing that it is an evil thing to desire many things at once — remembering the campaign of Cyrus against the Massagetae and what came of it, and the campaign of Cambyses against the Ethiopians, and being myself one who took part with Darius in the Scythian expedition. Knowing these things, I was of the opinion that you were to be envied of all men so long as you kept still. Since, however, there comes a divine impulse, and, it seems, a heaven-sent destruction is taking hold of the Greeks, I for my part both change my mind and reverse my opinions. Make known to the Persians the message that has been sent to you from God: bid them follow the commands you first gave about the preparations. Try, for your own part, that nothing be lacking, since God is putting the matter into your hands.” When these things had been said, both were inspired with confidence by the vision, and as soon as day came Xerxes communicated the matter to the Persians, and Artabanus, who before had been the only one stepping forward to dissuade him, now stepped forward to urge on the plan.
